User: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm married filing jointly, live in Portland OR. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $22,100 doing consulting for 3 clients, got $920 interest from Marcus savings account and $195 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $2,700 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $800 to Doctors Without Borders have the receipt, and had $650 in work sup

plies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
Assistant: Thanks — that’s a clear set of facts. Below I’ll go through what’s deductible, how to treat the home office, which forms to use, and whether you’ll probably take the standard deduction or itemize. If you want, I can run a rough tax calculation next (federal + self-employment tax + likely QBI deduction) — I’ll need one or two extra details (listed at the end).

Summary / quick answer
- For fed

eral 2023, you will almost certainly take the standard deduction (Married Filing Jointly = $27,700) unless you have substantial additional itemizable amounts (state/local tax or mortgage interest, etc.). With only the $800 charitable gift listed, itemizing is unlikely to beat $27,700.
- You should report the $22,100 consulting income on Schedule C (self‑employment). That allows you to deduct business expenses (the $650 supplies) and a home‑office deduction (if you meet the rules). Those business deductions

lower your AGI and taxable income regardless of whether you itemize.
- You can deduct up to $2,500 of student loan interest as an above‑the‑line adjustment (you paid $2,700, so the deduction is capped at $2,500), assuming you meet the income/eligibility rules.
- Report the interest ($920) and dividends ($195) on your Form 1040 (Schedule B only if combined interest + ordinary dividends > $1,500 or certain other conditions).
- Expect to pay self‑employment tax on net self‑employment income; you’ll also get a

deduction for half of the SE tax.

Details and how to report each item

1) Standard vs. itemize
- 2023 standard deduction (Married Filing Jointly): $27,700.
- Known potential itemized items you listed: charitable cash gift $800.
- Common other itemizable items that could change the decision: state income tax paid or state withholding, property taxes, mortgage interest, large medical expenses, large unreimbursed casualty losses. Because you did not list any of those, the standard deduction is almost certainl

y larger. If you provide state tax withholding or property tax paid, I can compute precisely.

2) Self‑employment income and business deductions (consulting)
- Report the $22,100 on Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business).
- Deductible business expenses: the $650 of work supplies is deductible on Schedule C.
- Self‑employment tax: use Schedule SE to compute SE tax (~15.3% on net self‑employment income). You may also deduct half of the SE tax on Form 1040 as an adjustment to income.
- Qualified Business In

come (QBI) deduction: you’ll likely be eligible for a Section 199A QBI deduction of up to 20% of qualified business income from your consulting, subject to rules. Because your taxable income is well below 2023 thresholds, this is probably available — I can estimate it.

3) Home office
- Because your consulting appears to be self‑employment (not an employee performing W‑2 work), you can use a home-office deduction if the office meets the rules:
  - Exclusive and regular use of the space for business.
  - Pri

ncipal place of business (or used to meet clients or for business purposes).
- You gave: home office = 165 sq ft, total home = 690 sq ft → business percentage = 165/690 ≈ 23.9%.
- Two methods:
  - Simplified: $5 per sq ft × 165 sq ft = $825 deduction (no Form 8829).
  - Actual expense method: allocate a percentage of actual home expenses to the business. For example, rent $2,050/mo = $24,600/year × 23.9% ≈ $5,880 (plus share of utilities, renter’s insurance, etc.). To use actual expenses and claim depreciat

ion (if you owned), you would file Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) with Schedule C. For renters, depreciation on the building does not apply, but rent and utilities are prorated.
- Practical note: the actual method usually yields a larger deduction here (because of high rent), but the home‑office deduction cannot exceed your net profit from the business (i.e., you can’t create a deductible business loss solely from the home office in certain circumstances — there are rules/limitations). G

iven your numbers, actual expenses likely fit under net self‑employment income, but I can check with a calculation.
- Important: Home office deductions are only available for the self‑employment portion. If you’re a W‑2 employee doing some work at home, unreimbursed employee expenses are not deductible federally (suspended through 2025).

4) Student loan interest
- Up to $2,500 of student loan interest is deductible as an adjustment to income (reported on Form 1040, via Schedule 1). You paid $2,700 in 2023,

so expect a $2,500 deduction if you meet the income limits and the loan is a qualified student loan.
- Eligibility: phaseout for MFJ in 2023 begins at MAGI $145,000 and phases out by $175,000. Your combined income (wages + self‑employment + interest/dividends) is about $108k, so you should be eligible for the full $2,500.

5) Interest and dividends
- Report $920 interest and $195 ordinary dividends on Form 1040. If combined interest + ordinary dividends > $1,500, attach Schedule B; otherwise, direct lines

on 1040 suffice. Expect 1099‑INT and 1099‑DIV forms from the banks/insurers.

6) Charitable contribution
- $800 cash gift to Doctors Without Borders is deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A) and the organization is a qualified charity. Keep the receipt. There is no “above‑the‑line” charitable deduction for 2023 if you don’t itemize.

7) Forms and worksheets you will use
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040) — adjustments to income (student loan interest, half of SE tax adjustment is on Fo

rm 1040 as well).
- Schedule C (Form 1040) — report consulting income and business expenses (supplies, home office deduction reported here).
- Schedule SE — compute self‑employment tax.
- Form 8829 — use only if you use the actual expenses method for the home office (to compute allowable business‑use‑of‑home expenses). If you use the simplified method, you do NOT file Form 8829.
- Schedule A — only if you choose to itemize (charitable contributions, state/local taxes up to SALT cap, mortgage interest, etc.)

.
- Schedule B — only if required (interest/dividends threshold or foreign accounts).
- Keep 1099‑NEC or 1099‑MISC (or client records), 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV, and any 1098‑E (student loan interest statement) or lender records.

Other practical points
- State taxes: Oregon has different rules; you’ll file an Oregon return and may be able to deduct state taxes on Schedule A (subject to SALT cap), but state tax rules for student loan interest, etc., can differ. I can help approximate state tax if you want.
- Esti

mated tax payments: because you had self‑employment income, you may owe self‑employment tax and may owe estimated payments if withholding insufficient. For 2024 planning, consider making quarterly estimated payments.
- Records: keep receipts for charitable gifts, student loan statements or payment records, invoices/records for consulting income, and records supporting the home office (floorplan, photos, utility bills) in case of audit.

Would you like me to:
- Run a driven estimate that compares (a) taking

the standard deduction vs (b) itemizing if you give me state income tax/property tax/mortgage interest numbers, and that also (c) compares simplified vs actual home office methods? If so, please confirm:
  - State tax withheld or paid in 2023 (Oregon), and property taxes (if any) or mortgage interest paid; and
  - Do your consulting clients have/issue 1099‑NEC or were you paid via other means?
I can then compute approximate federal taxable income, federal income tax, self‑employment tax, and show the tax im
pact of the home office and QBI.
